description: This entry covers What Genomics Studies as part of the fundamentals of genomics. In this field, dna sequencing matters because reading base order, from Sanger to massively parallel next-generation methods. It is taught at the Foundations level of the teaching ladder, building from first principles toward professional practice, with each concept defined before it is used.
overview: Genomics is the field concerned with Reading whole genomes: sequencing, assembly, and the data science of all of an organism's DNA. What Genomics Studies belongs to its essential core. Concretely: DNA sequencing — reading base order, from Sanger to massively parallel next-generation methods. And Variant calling — spotting SNPs and indels differing from a reference genome. Mastering this entry means being able to explain the topic in plain sentences, recognize it in real cases, and apply it alongside the neighboring ideas of the Foundations tier.
core_concepts: DNA sequencing: reading base order, from Sanger to massively parallel next-generation methods.
Variant calling: spotting SNPs and indels differing from a reference genome.
key_laws: Lander-Waterman statistics: coverage depth predicting assembly completeness.
vocabulary: Read: one sequenced DNA fragment, tens to millions of bases long.
SNP: a single-base variant between individuals.
methods: Library preparation: fragmenting and barcoding DNA for the sequencer.
history: Genomics began with Sanger sequencing in 1977; the 2003 Human Genome Project finished the first human reference. Next-generation sequencing crashed costs a million-fold, and genomics now spans medicine, agriculture, and microbiome science.
